summary: Specifies the file transfer protocol, a user-level protocol for moving files between hosts on the ARPANET, including terminal IMPs. Its main goal is to make transferring files and using remote storage easy. It updates RFC 114 and was replaced by RFC 265.

eli5.summary: A helper that copies files from one computer to another. You tell it what you want, and it fetches or sends the file for you.

subtitle: The 1971 ARPANET file transfer protocol, built on opcodes sent over one connection.

tldr.problem: ARPANET hosts had different file systems, and users needed a standard way to move and store files on other hosts.
tldr.mechanism: FTP sends binary control transactions, identified by an op code in the first byte, over the data transfer protocol of RFC 171, with requests such as retrieve, store, delete and rename.
tldr.outcome: This early FTP specification updates RFC 114 and has been replaced by RFC 265, which was itself updated by RFC 238.

today: RFC 172 is an early specification that updated RFC 114 and has been replaced by RFC 265. It was itself updated by RFC 238.

sections.title: Goals and Design
sections.content:
The file transfer protocol (FTP) is a user-level protocol for moving files between host computers on the ARPA network, including terminal IMPs. It uses the data transfer protocol of RFC 171 and assumes the reader knows it.

The objectives are to promote sharing of files, encourage indirect use of computers without login, and shield the user from variations in file and storage systems. FTP does not restrict what a file holds and offers no standard pathname convention yet. Each user follows the naming rules of the file system being used. Access control is limited to username and password identifiers.
sections.eli5: Different computers store files in different ways. FTP gives them one common way to ask for and hand over files.

sections.title: Control Transactions and Op Codes
sections.content:
Data and control transactions travel over the same connection. Data transactions carry file contents only; the structure of the data is conveyed by control transactions. Control transactions are told apart by their first byte, the op code, and are requests, identifiers or terminates.

Requests include retrieve (01), store (02), delete (03), rename_from (04), rename_to (05), list_file_directory (06) and append (0B). Identifiers include username (07), password (08) and change data type (00). Codes 09 and 0A in the table are the error and acknowledge terminates. Op codes hex 5A through FF are for experimental use.
sections.eli5: The first byte of every message is like a button label saying what you want: get, save, delete, rename, or list.

sections.title: Requests, Data Types and Errors
sections.content:
A retrieve request copies a file from the serving host and leaves the original unchanged. A store request carries a 4-byte allocate size field (0 means the server uses its default) and replaces an existing file or creates a new one. Append adds data to an existing file. A rename_from must always be followed by a rename_to.

The change data type transaction describes the structure of following data. The default is a bit stream with byte size 1. Other assigned types include binary bytes, network ASCII, EBCDIC and decimal, octal and hexadecimal numbers. A host must accept data even if it does not recognize the type. Error terminates carry a code in the second byte, such as name syntax error, access control violation, abort and opcode not implemented.
sections.eli5: Getting a file leaves the original alone. Saving a file puts a copy on the other computer, and if something goes wrong the other computer sends back an error number.

sections.title: Order of Transactions and Connections
sections.content:
Identifier transactions (data type, username, password) may be sent at any time and are not acknowledged. The usual order is username then password at the start of the connection. After a retrieve or list, the server sends the file and then an end-of-file indication. After a store or append, the user sends the file and an end-of-file indication, and the server must acknowledge. Rename and delete also require an acknowledge.

Either host may abort a request at any time with an error terminate, or more drastically by closing the connection. The cooperating process at the serving host listens on a preassigned permanent socket, and a connection is made with the standard initial connection protocol. A footnote suggests socket 3 seems a reasonable choice for file transfer.
sections.eli5: You say who you are, make a request, and the other side sends the file or says done. Either side can hang up if there is a big problem.

messages.label: Acknowledge
messages.note: Receipt of the file must be acknowledged.
